clips.text: A busy counter in Mexico often has no formal line at all — just a cluster of people, and whoever makes eye contact and speaks up gets served next. Standing back quietly, the way you might queue at home, can mean waiting a very long time.
You're the fourth person deep at a busy taco stand, no line, everyone talking over everyone. The cook glances up. This is the half-second that matters.
¿Quién sigue?
That question is your opening, not a formality to survive. Answer it immediately, at a normal speaking volume — not a whisper, not a shout.
The cook asks who's next. Claim your turn immediately. Speak now.
Yo sigo, por favor.
Dígame.
If two people speak at once and it isn't clear who was actually first, this line settles it without an argument.
Creo que yo llegué primero.
Someone else also claims the turn. Say, calmly, that you think you arrived first. Speak now.

Here's the permission this whole part is built on. The English instinct — 'I was wondering if I could possibly...' — doesn't read as polite here. It reads as distance, and it makes the cook wonder if you're actually ready to order.
¿Qué le doy?
Order directly, no padding, no apology for existing. Speak now.
Deme dos de pastor, por favor.
Yo sigo, por favor. Creo que yo llegué primero. Deme dos de pastor, por favor.

I02 complete. No formal line, no problem: yo sigo claims your turn, creo que yo llegué primero defends it if needed, and a direct deme plus what you want is the whole order. Quiet waiting was never the polite move — speaking up, at a normal volume, was.
A crowded taco stand with no formal line. Listen for how the traveller claims a turn and orders directly.
¿Quién sigue?
Yo sigo, por favor.
¿Qué le doy?
Deme dos de pastor, por favor.
